body.heading: Why stepping out works so fast
paragraphs: Stress narrows everything: the visual field shrinks to the screen, the thoughts shrink to the problem, time shrinks to the deadline. Stepping outside reverses all three at once. The horizon widens, the air changes, the body moves, and the sky — reliably, indifferently enormous — puts the problem back to scale.
None of this requires nature in the grand sense. A doorstep, a balcony, a pavement with one tree will do. The active ingredient is the change of scene and the distance in the view, not wilderness.

body.heading: How to take your minute
paragraphs: Go out and do as little as possible, on purpose. Look at the furthest thing you can see. Feel the temperature on your face. Listen for the most distant sound, then the nearest. Let your breathing slow down to match the pace of the outdoors, which is in no hurry at all.

Leave the phone inside, or at least in your pocket. Sixty seconds is short enough that nothing will be missed, and the minute works partly because it is unmediated — just you and the weather, like most of human history.

body.heading: Make it a reflex worth having
paragraphs: Attach the minute to moments that reliably need it: after the difficult call, before the tense meeting, when you catch yourself reading the same paragraph for the fourth time. The earlier in a spiral you step out, the less unwinding there is to do.
On days when going out is impossible, the window is a decent deputy: stand at it, look far, breathe slowly. It is not the same, but it points the same direction — out.

takeaway: One minute, real sky, furthest view: the smallest possible change of scene.
